statement: The supplied sources contain no derivation of the binomial coefficient, introducing it instead as a foundational mathematical definition and object. For non-negative integers n and k with n >= k >= 0, the binomial coefficient \binom{n}{k} is defined as the positive integer occurring as the coefficient in the binomial theorem. Algebraically, for an integer or real f and non-negative integer k, it is defined via the falling factorial as \binom{f}{k} = \frac{(f)_k}{k!} = \frac{(f-k+1)\cdots(f-1)f}{1\cdot 2\cdots k}, and generalized to real or complex arguments x, y via the gamma function as \binom{x}{y} = \frac{\Gamma(x+1)}{\Gamma(y+1)\Gamma(x-y+1)} = \frac{1}{(x+1)\mathrm{B}(y+1,x-y+1)}.

assumptions.assumption: In the standard combinatorial definition, n and k are integers satisfying n >= k >= 0
assumptions.breaks_when: Arguments are negative, non-integers, or k > n, requiring extension to falling factorials or gamma/beta functions
|z| >= 1, where the series exceeds its radius of convergence

assumptions.assumption: In the gamma function generalization, x+1, y+1, and x-y+1 must not create uncancelled poles
assumptions.breaks_when: x is a negative integer and y is not an integer, leading to singularities

failure_modes.mode: Series divergence in Newton's binomial series
failure_modes.signature: Infinite terms grow without bound and the series fails to converge to (1+z)^\alpha
failure_modes.cause: Evaluating the series for arguments |z| > 1 outside the radius of convergence

failure_modes.signature: Gamma function evaluates to infinity / division by zero
failure_modes.cause: Evaluating \binom{x}{y} where negative integer poles of \Gamma(x+1) are not cancelled by denominator poles

failure_modes.mode: Failure of classical symmetry identity under generalization
failure_modes.cause: Applying standard non-negative integer symmetry \binom{n}{m} = \binom{n}{n-m} outside its valid domain
